prompt: Scientist 1 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.text: The temperature difference is greater on holidays than it is on busy weekdays.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the difference shrinks on holidays; Scientist 1 does not discuss it.

choices.text: Waste heat from vehicles and buildings is the main reason the city is warm at night.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's explanation.

choices.text: The temperature difference is largest in winter, when heating systems run.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the difference is smallest in winter.

choices.text: Replacing pavement with vegetation would lower nighttime temperatures in the city.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says vegetation cools the air and recommends planting trees.

explanation: Scientist 1 attributes the warmth to materials and the loss of vegetation, so adding vegetation should help.

stimulus.title: The Warm City
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The city center is about 4°C warmer at night than the surrounding farmland because of what the city is made of. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and store the heat, releasing it slowly after sunset. These surfaces are also dark, so they reflect less sunlight than fields and forests do. Vegetation cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, but the city has replaced most plants with pavement. The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights, when stored heat is released most effectively, and smallest in winter, when the sun is weak. Painting roofs white and planting trees would reduce the difference.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The warmth comes mainly from the energy people use. Every engine, air conditioner, furnace, and light releases heat into the city's air. In the dense center, this waste heat per square kilometer can rival the energy delivered by sunlight. The nighttime difference is large because the city keeps releasing heat after the sun sets, while the countryside does not. The difference also grows on weekdays, when traffic and business activity are heaviest, and shrinks on holidays, something that building materials alone cannot explain. Reducing energy use and improving the efficiency of vehicles and buildings would do more than changing roof colors.

prompt: Both scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: material beneath the road was removed before the collapse occurred.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 describes dissolved limestone and Scientist 2 describes washed-away soil, but both describe a void forming first.

choices.text: the collapse was caused by rainwater that had become slightly acidic.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 cites acidic rainwater.

choices.text: the water main under the road is cracked.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 reports the cracked main.

choices.text: the hole's walls are made of solid limestone.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the walls are mostly loose soil.

explanation: Both views involve a void forming beneath the pavement; they differ on how it formed.

stimulus.title: The Collapse at Carver Road
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The sudden hole that opened beneath Carver Road formed because rainwater slowly dissolved the limestone beneath the surface. Limestone is made of a mineral that dissolves in slightly acidic water, and rain becomes acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil. Over thousands of years, water seeping down through cracks widened them into a cavern. The roof of the cavern thinned until it could no longer hold up the road. Caves and springs are common in the surrounding countryside, and the hole has sheer walls of solid limestone, exactly as expected when a cavern roof gives way.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The hole formed because a leaking water main washed away the soil beneath the road. The main, installed sixty years ago, runs directly under the collapse and was found to be cracked. Escaping water carried fine soil particles into a nearby storm drain, leaving a growing void just below the pavement. Limestone caverns take thousands of years to form, but the road showed no sign of sinking until two months before the collapse, soon after water pressure in the main was raised. The hole's walls are mostly loose soil, and the solid rock lies several meters deeper. Repairing the main is the key to preventing another collapse.

prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: The nighttime temperature difference became much smaller during a week-long power outage.
choices.rationale: Correct. Less energy use with the same buildings leading to a smaller difference points to waste heat as the cause.

choices.text: The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights and smallest in winter.
choices.rationale: This pattern is what Scientist 1 predicts from stored sunlight.

choices.text: Tree-lined streets are cooler at night than streets without trees.
choices.rationale: Cooling by trees supports Scientist 1's emphasis on vegetation.

choices.text: Dark roofs are measured to be hotter than light-colored roofs at sunset.
choices.rationale: Hot dark roofs support the materials explanation.

explanation: Scientist 2's claim is that energy use drives the warmth; a drop in warmth when energy use drops supports it.

prompt: Suppose a city with very little industry or traffic, but built of the same materials, showed the same nighttime temperature difference as a busy city of similar size. This finding would most likely:

choices.text: support both viewpoints about equally.
choices.rationale: The finding contradicts the waste-heat explanation.

choices.text: support Scientist 2's viewpoint and weaken Scientist 1's.
choices.rationale: Low energy use with the same warmth argues against waste heat as the cause.

choices.text: support Scientist 1's viewpoint and weaken Scientist 2's.
choices.rationale: Correct. The same warmth with far less energy use suggests materials, not waste heat, are responsible.

choices.text: weaken both viewpoints to the same degree.
choices.rationale: The finding is consistent with the materials explanation.

explanation: If energy use varies greatly but the warmth does not, materials are the better explanation.

prompt: The central disagreement between the two scientists concerns:

choices.text: whether the sun changes its position in the sky over the course of a day.
choices.rationale: Both accept that the sun moves; Scientist 1 even uses this to explain misdirected bees.

choices.text: whether bees' bodies contain grains of the magnetic mineral magnetite.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not dispute the presence of magnetite, only its importance.

choices.text: whether bees are able to find their way back to the hive from unfamiliar, distant places.
choices.rationale: Both accept that bees navigate home successfully.

choices.text: whether bees' main directional cue comes from the sky or from the magnetic field.
choices.rationale: Correct. Sun and polarized light versus the magnetic field is the central dispute.

explanation: The disagreement is about the main cue, not about whether bees navigate or whether magnetite exists.

stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.

prompt: Which of the following observations, if confirmed, would provide the strongest support for Scientist 1's explanation?

choices.text: The fungus is found on healthy frogs in remote regions with no farming.
choices.rationale: Healthy carriers are Scientist 2's evidence that the fungus alone is not enough.

choices.text: Frogs at sites downwind of farms decline faster than frogs upwind.
choices.rationale: A downwind pattern supports the pesticide explanation.

choices.text: Captive frogs never exposed to pesticides die when infected with the fungus.
choices.rationale: Correct. Death without any pesticide exposure shows the fungus can kill on its own, as Scientist 1 claims.

choices.text: Pesticide residues are detected in snow collected at high elevations in the mountains.
choices.rationale: Residues in snow support Scientist 2's claim that pesticides reach the mountains.

explanation: Scientist 1 claims the fungus alone is lethal; deaths of frogs with no pesticide exposure demonstrate exactly that.

stimulus.title: The Vanishing Frogs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Frog populations in mountain streams across the region have crashed because of a fungus that infects amphibian skin. Frogs breathe and take in water partly through their skin, and the infection disrupts this exchange until the heart fails. The fungus has been found on dead frogs at every site where populations collapsed, and healthy populations remain only where the fungus is absent. Declines have spread from valley to valley in a wave, the way a contagious disease spreads, and have hit protected parks with clean water as hard as farmland. Frogs raised in captivity and exposed to the fungus die within weeks.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The declines are the result of pesticides carried by wind and rain from farms into the mountains. Pesticide residues have been measured in stream water, in frog tissue, and even in snow at high elevations. These chemicals weaken the frogs' immune systems, which is why a fungus that frogs have lived with for a long time now kills them. The fungus is found on many healthy frogs in regions with little agriculture, so its presence alone does not cause collapse. Declines are also most severe at sites downwind of major farming areas. Reducing pesticide drift would let the frogs resist the fungus as they once did.
